findings.claim: Cities such as Dar es Salaam (Tanzania), Luanda (Angola) and Lahore (Pakistan) are among those expected to cross the 10 million threshold.
findings.truth: Lahore is already a megacity — UN DESA puts it at about 15.2 million, and it was over 10 million in the 2018 UN revision. Dar es Salaam and Luanda are still below 10 million.

findings.claim: Brazil has a tropical savannah climate, and Rio's average temperatures range between 21-27C.
findings.truth: Brazil spans several climate zones (equatorial rainforest in the north, humid subtropical in the south). It is Rio itself that has a tropical savannah climate.
findings.evidence: Koppen classification; Wikipedia, Rio de Janeiro

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'Brazils'.
findings.truth: The apostrophe was stripped from 'Brazil's' when the cloze was generated.

findings.claim: Murder rates are high - around 20 per 1,000.
findings.truth: Homicide rates are given per 100,000. Brazil's national rate was 20.1 per 100,000 in 2022 and Rio city 35.7 per 100,000 in 2007. 20 per 1,000 is 100 times too high.

findings.claim: Card: '_____ and Unemployment Education is compulsory for ages 6-14...' with answer 'Education'.
findings.truth: The answer word sits inside its own question and a heading was glued to the sentence.

findings.claim: a cable car system linking the hilltop favela to the commercial centre of Ipanema.
findings.truth: The Teleferico do Alemao ran 3.5 km from Palmeiras to Bonsucesso station on the SuperVia rail network, in the North Zone. Ipanema is a beach district about 20 km away and is not a commercial centre.

findings.claim: In Complexo do Alemao (home to 26,000 people).
findings.truth: The 2010 census counted 69,143 residents in Complexo do Alemao.

findings.claim: Curitiba is a city of around 1.9 million people in south-east Brazil. Under Mayor Jaime Lerner (1971-2001).
findings.truth: Curitiba is in Parana, in Brazil's South Region. Lerner was mayor three times (1971-74, 1979-83, 1989-92); 1995-2002 he was governor of Parana, not mayor.

findings.claim: Two cards built from headings: 'The _____ Bairro Scheme...' (answer 'Favela') and '_____ The $1 billion budget...' (answer 'Limitations').
findings.truth: The first repeats its answer in the question; the second cannot be answered from the prompt.

findings.claim: Liverpool has 11 universities (repeated in lessons 5 and 7, the key fact, conclusion, exam tip, two mark schemes and a knowledge check).
findings.truth: Liverpool has three universities: the University of Liverpool, Liverpool John Moores University and Liverpool Hope University. LIPA and the School of Tropical Medicine are specialist colleges, not universities.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of universities in the United Kingdom

findings.claim: The Albert Dock ... is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
findings.truth: Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City was inscribed in 2004 and removed from the World Heritage list in 2021 after the Bramley-Moore Dock stadium and Liverpool Waters approvals.

findings.claim: By the early 20th century, the city handled around 40% of the world's trade.
findings.truth: The 40% share is attributed to the 19th century, when the docks were at their peak.

findings.claim: Card: 'Key Fact _____ 80% of the UK's population lives in urban areas' with answer 'Over'.
findings.truth: The card carries the 'Key Fact' label and a one-word answer that teaches nothing.

findings.claim: Around 1.3 million Irish people moved to Liverpool.
findings.truth: About 1.3 million passed through the port during the famine years, most sailing on to North America. Liverpool held about 90,000 Irish-born residents in 1851 out of roughly 376,000 people.
findings.evidence: 1851 census figures quoted in the lesson itself; Wikipedia, Liverpool

findings.claim: 2,500 people were killed in one week in May [1941].
findings.truth: The May Blitz (1-7 May 1941) caused 2,895 casualties, of whom 1,741 were killed and 1,154 injured.

findings.claim: 184 of Liverpool's 257 dock berths were damaged or destroyed.
findings.truth: The raids put 69 of the port's 144 cargo berths out of action.

findings.claim: It sustained heavy damage during the May Blitz of 1941, and by the 1950s the repair costs were too high to justify.
findings.truth: A 1955 survey found the iron deck badly corroded by steam and soot from the dock lines; repairs would have cost 2 million pounds, which the company could not raise, so it closed in 1956.

findings.claim: dating from 1834 when immigrants arrived to work for the Blue Funnel shipping line (Alfred Holt and Company).
findings.truth: The 1834 arrival was the first ship sailing direct from China. Alfred Holt's Blue Funnel Line began in the 1860s and brought the later waves of Chinese sailors.

findings.claim: the ornate Chinatown arch on Nelson Street - the largest outside China (twice).
findings.truth: At 13.5 m it is the tallest Chinatown arch in Europe and the second tallest outside mainland China; the Washington DC arch is taller.

findings.claim: Between 1846 and 1852, the Irish Potato Famine caused mass starvation.
findings.truth: The famine ran 1845-1852, as the lesson's own glossary definition states. The knowledge-check option repeated 1846.

findings.claim: Card: '3 million _____ people moved to Liverpool' with answer 'Irish'; a second card also answers 'Irish'.
findings.truth: The cloze cut '1.' off '1.3 million', so the card teaches a figure three times too large, and two cards in one deck share an answer.
findings.evidence: lesson content_html; validator rule on duplicate answers

findings.claim: Green corridors along the Liverpool & Leeds Canal.
findings.truth: The waterway is the Leeds and Liverpool Canal.
findings.evidence: Canal and River Trust naming; Wikipedia, Leeds and Liverpool Canal

findings.claim: Card: '_____ Capital of Culture 2008 Liverpool was awarded the European Capital of Culture in 2008' with answer 'European'.
findings.truth: The answer word appears in its own question.

findings.claim: Card: '_____ Regeneration The 260 million pound regeneration of Anfield...' with answer 'Anfield'.
findings.truth: The answer word appears in its own question.

findings.claim: the UK has a GNI per capita of 42,130 pounds while Nepal has just 1,020 pounds.
findings.truth: Those are US dollar values (World Bank Atlas method); the UK figure in pounds would be about 33,000.
findings.evidence: World Bank GNI per capita series

findings.claim: Card: 'Key Fact In the _____ the Brandt Line divided the world into the "rich north" and "poor south' (quotation left unclosed).
findings.truth: The card carries the 'Key Fact' label and a broken quotation.

findings.claim: Card: 'The _____ Gap The development gap refers to...' with answer 'Development'.
findings.truth: The answer word appears in its own question.

findings.claim: Card: '2 million barrels of oil per day globally...'.
findings.truth: The lesson text says Shell extracts 3.2 million barrels a day; the cloze cut '3.' off the figure.

findings.claim: Tourism ... employs approximately 500,000 people - around 10% of the population (repeated in the key fact and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: Kenya's population is about 54 million, so 500,000 jobs is roughly 1% of the population. The 10% figure that circulates refers to employment, not population, so the claim as written is false.

findings.claim: Debt relief is taught under 'Bottom-Up Development Strategies' and listed as bottom-up in the collapsible and the conclusion.
findings.truth: Debt relief is agreed by national governments and international bodies (the G8 and the IMF/World Bank MDRI), so it is a top-down strategy. The lesson's own description of top-down as government-led contradicts its placing.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.2 strategy list; lesson's own definitions

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'Chinas'.
findings.truth: The apostrophe was stripped from 'China's'.

findings.claim: the partition of India ... divided the subcontinent into three countries: India, Pakistan and Bangladesh (also in the glossary, a flashcard and a knowledge check).
findings.truth: Partition in 1947 created two states, India and Pakistan (Pakistan in two wings). East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971.

findings.claim: Since 1950, India has had 19 prime ministers.
findings.truth: India has had 14 prime ministers.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of prime ministers of India

findings.claim: from around 400 million in 1950 to over 1.4 billion today - an increase of 1 billion people in just 60 years.
findings.truth: 1950 to the present is about 75 years.

findings.claim: Mumbai receives 1,304 mm of rain per year, while New Delhi receives only 536 mm.
findings.truth: Mumbai averages 2,502 mm a year; New Delhi averages 774 mm.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia climate boxes, Mumbai and New Delhi

findings.claim: Two cards in the deck both answer 'India', one prefixed 'Key Fact'.
findings.truth: Two flashcards in one lesson must not share an answer.

findings.claim: Between 2018 and 2019, India's GDP increased by 257%.
findings.truth: India's GDP grew about 5% in that year. Measured from 2010 it has roughly doubled (1.68 trillion dollars in 2010 to over 3.5 trillion by 2023).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Economy of India; World Bank GDP series

findings.claim: India's exports are worth approximately $115 billion, while its imports cost $228 billion ... a deficit of $113 billion.
findings.truth: The lesson's own country breakdown (USA $72bn + UAE $25bn + China $23bn + Bangladesh $14bn) already exceeds the stated export total. India's trade runs at about $860 billion of exports against $979 billion of imports, a deficit near $119 billion.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Economy of India (FY2025-26 merchandise trade)

findings.claim: Cards prefixed 'Key Fact In _____' and '_____ this to the UK...' with answer 'Compare'.
findings.truth: One carries the label, the other has an answer that is not a geography fact.

findings.claim: India is now the third-largest steel importer and the second-largest steel exporter in the world, having increased production by 75% since 2008.
findings.truth: India is the world's second-largest steel producer (since January 2019) and is a net importer of steel, not a leading exporter. Output rose from 101.5 Mt in 2017 to 144.3 Mt in 2023-24.

findings.claim: Coal use has increased from 200 million metric tonnes in 1980 to 1,800 million metric tonnes in 2021 - a difference of 1,600 million tonnes (repeated in the key fact, conclusion, exam tip and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: India consumed 906 million tonnes of coal in 2020-21 and mined 1,047 million tonnes in FY2024-25. The 1,800 million tonne figure is roughly double the real one.

findings.claim: Life expectancy has risen from 38 years to 68 years within a single generation.
findings.truth: That rise runs from about 1950 to today, roughly 70 years, not one generation.
findings.evidence: UN life expectancy series for India

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'COVID19'.
findings.truth: The hyphen was stripped from COVID-19.

findings.claim: Two cards in the deck both answer 'Stage', both built from timeline headings.
findings.truth: Two flashcards in one lesson must not share an answer, and neither prompt is answerable.

findings.claim: Cambridge Science Park was jointly built by Cambridge University and the local authority.
findings.truth: Trinity College, Cambridge created the park in 1970 on its own land.

findings.claim: Card: '_____ The cement works contributes around 9 million pounds...' with answer 'Advantages'.
findings.truth: A heading fragment left the card unanswerable.

findings.claim: Heathrow is already the UK's largest emitter of CO&sub2.
findings.truth: Broken entity: the page shows the literal text 'CO&sub2' to students. It should read CO2 with a subscript.

findings.claim: Heathrow handles approximately 480,000 flights and 73 million passengers per year.
findings.truth: Heathrow handled 473,965 flights and 83,859,729 passengers in 2024. The flight figure is right, so 73 million is internally inconsistent with it.

findings.claim: The Commonwealth is an association of 53 countries with nearly 2 billion people (30% of the world's population); the same lesson's definition says 56 countries.
findings.truth: The Commonwealth has 56 member states and about 2.42 billion people, which is roughly 30% of the world.

findings.claim: Gas produces less CO&sub2 than coal when burned.
findings.truth: Broken entity, as in lesson 17.

findings.claim: Card: '_____ For Fracking Fracking creates a more reliable energy supply...' with answer 'Arguments'.
findings.truth: A heading fragment left the card unanswerable.

findings.claim: Liverpool ONE has '3,000 underground car parking spaces', but lesson 7 teaches that Chavasse Park sits above a 2,000-space underground car park, and its knowledge check tests 2,000.
findings.truth: One of the two figures is wrong and a student meets both. Published Liverpool ONE material says over 2,000 spaces, so my recommendation is to change lesson 8 to 2,000 and leave lesson 7 alone - but the site's own capacity pages should be checked before the edit.

findings.claim: Cuba has a literacy rate of 99.7% but a low GDP, while the Maldives has a high GDP but a lower literacy rate.
findings.truth: Maldives literacy is around 98% and its HDI is 0.766 (high), so the contrast teaches a false impression of poor Maldivian education. The point about single indicators still stands; my recommendation is to swap the Maldives for a state with genuinely weak social indicators against high income (for example Equatorial Guinea).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Maldives (HDI 0.766, GDP per capita PPP $34,322)

findings.claim: Goa ... 140,000 tourists visited in 2022-2023, creating a positive multiplier effect with 250,000-300,000 jobs.
findings.truth: Goa's total arrivals run to several million a year; 140,000 can only be foreign arrivals, and as written it cannot support 250,000-300,000 jobs. My recommendation is to label the figure 'international tourists' or replace it with a sourced total from Goa Tourism.
findings.evidence: internal implausibility; Wikipedia, Goa (no arrivals figure published there)

findings.claim: Castle Cement is ... recycling 100 million tonnes of waste products.
findings.truth: The works makes 750,000 tonnes of cement a year, so 100 million tonnes of recycled waste is impossible - most likely 100,000 tonnes. I could not find the company figure, so it needs checking with Hanson before an edit.
findings.evidence: internal implausibility against the plant's stated output

findings.claim: In 2005, roughly 3.4 billion people lived in urban areas ... 6.5 billion by 2050; 34 megacities in 2020 rising to 50 by 2050.
findings.truth: UN World Urbanization Prospects gives about 3.2 billion urban in 2005, 6.7 billion by 2050, 33 megacities in 2018 and 43 projected for 2030; it publishes no 2050 megacity count. All within teaching tolerance.

findings.claim: Education is compulsory for ages 6-14 [in Brazil].
findings.truth: Brazil has required schooling from age 4 to 17 since the 2009 constitutional amendment, phased in by 2016. The 6-14 window is the older textbook figure.

findings.claim: Bi-articulated (bendy) buses carry up to 4,000 passengers per day.
findings.truth: Curitiba's bi-articulated buses are usually quoted at about 270 passengers each. I could not verify a per-day figure, so the number is left alone.

findings.claim: Liverpool attracts over 67 million visitors per year ... the Port of Liverpool handles 32 billion pounds of cargo annually; around 50,000 students.
findings.truth: The 67 million figure is the Liverpool City Region total including day trips. The port cargo value could not be verified. The three universities now enrol about 62,000 students between them, so 50,000 understates it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of universities in the United Kingdom (2024/25 student numbers)

findings.claim: over 10,000 homes were destroyed [in the May Blitz].
findings.truth: Wikipedia gives over 6,500 homes completely destroyed in that week, with about 10,000 for the Blitz as a whole. The edit softens this to 'thousands'.

findings.claim: House builders like Keep Moat ...; the council has invested 4 million pounds in tree planting.
findings.truth: The company is Keepmoat (one word). The tree-planting figure could not be verified.

findings.claim: HICs have a GNI per capita of $12,746 or above; LICs $1,045 or less.
findings.truth: Those are the World Bank's 2015 thresholds. The current ones are about $14,000 and $1,145. They are internally consistent and still taught, so they are left alone.

findings.claim: the NHS has over 65,000 nursing vacancies; malaria is found in South America, Central and Southern Africa, and South-East Asia.
findings.truth: NHS England nursing vacancies peaked near 47,000 and usually run around 40,000. Malaria's burden is overwhelmingly in West and East Africa, which the list omits.
findings.evidence: NHS Digital vacancy statistics; WHO malaria distribution

findings.claim: car manufacturing accounts for 35% of India's manufacturing GDP ... worth over $222 billion (higher than the entire GDP of Greece); SAFTA covers seven South Asian countries.
findings.truth: Indian industry bodies publish 49% of manufacturing GDP. Greece's GDP is now about $240 billion, so the comparison is marginal. SAFTA has eight members since Afghanistan joined in 2007.

findings.claim: 236,000 millionaires; 300 million people below $1.25 a day; rural poverty risen from 25% to 29.6% since 2012.
findings.truth: All three are dated. Wealth reports now count several hundred thousand dollar millionaires, the international poverty line is $2.15, and World Bank estimates show rural poverty falling. They remain teachable as textbook figures.
findings.evidence: World Bank poverty and inequality platform

findings.claim: From 1945 to 1975, most UK industries were state-owned.
findings.truth: Nationalisation covered coal, rail, steel, utilities and a few others, not most of the economy.

findings.claim: average pay 28,000 pounds south against 24,000 north, unemployment 4.7% against 8.1%; the BBC relocated to MediaCity UK in Manchester.
findings.truth: The pay, house-price and unemployment figures are a decade old (UK unemployment has not been 8.1% in the north for years). MediaCityUK is in Salford, within Greater Manchester.

findings.claim: Fossil fuels account for around 87% of all energy production; the remaining 13% comes from renewable and nuclear sources. Lesson 20 says non-renewables including nuclear are the 87% and renewables the 13%.
findings.truth: Fossil fuels are now about 82% of global primary energy, nuclear about 4% and renewables about 14%. The two lessons also place nuclear on opposite sides of the split, which a student will notice.

findings.claim: three small earthquakes near Blackpool (magnitude 3 on the Richter Scale).
findings.truth: The tremors were magnitude 2.3 and 1.5 at Preese Hall in 2011 and 2.9 at Preston New Road in 2019. 'Magnitude 3' is a rounding, and the lesson's own key fact gives 2.9.

findings.claim: Nepal's ... entire population of 27 million people.
findings.truth: Nepal's 2021 census counted 29.16 million. 27 million is the 2011 figure.

summary: Exam claims are sound: every lesson's extended question is labelled 9 marks plus 3 SPaG, which matches the spec's Paper 2 (1h30, 88 marks including 3 for SPaG, 35%), no board is named in student-facing text and no paper or section codes appear. The content carries a heavy load of wrong figures instead: a murder rate given per 1,000 rather than per 100,000, Liverpool credited with 11 universities and a live UNESCO listing, Kenya's 500,000 tourism jobs called 10% of the population, partition splitting India into three countries, Indian GDP up 257% in one year, trade totals smaller than their own country breakdown, and the Rio cable car running to Ipanema. 51 findings are fixed in 102 edits, 4 need Tom's judgement and 15 are recorded as dated-but-teachable.
